message.content:
The sea usually looks **blue**—that’s the classic image people have in mind. The reason is that water absorbs colors at the red end of the spectrum more strongly than the blue end, so the blue wavelengths are scattered back to our eyes.  

However, the exact hue can vary a lot:

| Factor | Typical Color |
|--------|---------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water tends to look darker blue or even indigo. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | Greenish or turquoise tones appear when there’s a lot of microscopic plant life. |
| **Sediment & minerals** | Brownish or muddy hues can show up near river mouths or in shallow coastal areas. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | A bright midday sun gives a vivid blue; sunrise/sunset can turn it pink or orange. |
| **Human perception** | Our brains interpret the reflected light, so the same water can look different under different lighting conditions. |

So while “blue” is the most common description, the sea’s color is actually a dynamic mix that depends on depth, composition, and lighting.
